w1.summary: Hassan et al. map 18 themes that act as both barriers to and facilitators of AI adoption in health care, with trust at the centre and governance needed from conception to sustained use.
answers: Process. The five Arksey and O'Malley stages for scoping reviews: identify the question, find relevant studies, select studies, chart the data, and collate and report the results, guided by JBI methodology. The optional sixth stage, consulting stakeholders, was not done. Weak points to note: study selection changed as themes formed, and one author coded the themes (p.4).

Research question. Built with the population, concept, context approach and a deliberately broad context: 'What are the barriers to and facilitators of AI adoption in health care?' They added facilitators because a review of barriers alone (Assadullah) already existed, and no review covered both sides (p.3 to p.4).

Three core considerations. Ethics, bias, and transparency or explainability (p.10). This ranking is the authors' judgement from a scoping review, not a weighted result. Explainability matters most when the AI's reason would change what the clinician does.

Bias examples (p.11 to p.12). A vision algorithm that failed on dark skin because over 80% of the reference data were light-skinned; worse anti-sickness care for Black patients across 40 anaesthesia centres; chest X-ray models that underdiagnose Hispanic patients (CheXclusion); schizophrenia risk models trained on European populations failing in East Asian groups; and Obermeyer's algorithm that used cost as a proxy for need, so Black patients were judged less ill.

Both ways. When a theme such as explainability appeared as a barrier, the authors also recorded what the articles recommended to overcome it and tabulated that as the facilitator side of the same theme (p.5). This turns a list of problems into a list of actions. Governance is the exception, appearing only as a facilitator (p.6).

Four reasons to explain, from Adadi and Berrada 2018: explain to justify a decision, to control (find flaws and shortcuts), to improve the model, and to discover new knowledge. Any example that fits the definition works. Clinicians at the bedside usually need 'justify'; developers need 'control' and 'improve'.

Fixing bias (p.11). Define fairness and the deployment context first; reweigh or resample data from marginalised groups; train on diverse or local data; set comparable thresholds for each group, then monitor and retrain; watch for data set drift; use federated learning so data stay in each hospital. All are technical fixes. None would have caught Obermeyer's problem on its own, because the bias came from the choice of target (cost instead of need), which needs clinicians in the room when the target is chosen.

Trust. Trust is not one barrier among 18 but the hub that almost every theme feeds into, either building or damaging it (p.10, Figure 3 on p.13). Facilitators include endorsement by experts and regulators, evidence of accuracy, trusted clinical leaders and involving patients in development (p.7). Too much trust is also a risk: automation bias.

DeepMind and the Royal Free. In 2017 the Royal Free London NHS Foundation Trust gave Google DeepMind the records of about 1.6 million patients, without their consent, to test an app for detecting acute kidney injury (p.12); the Information Commissioner's Office ruled the trust had broken data protection law. On ownership, the paper names 'who owns the data' as an unresolved barrier (p.9). In UK law health data are generally not treated as property: the hospital is the data controller, and the patient holds rights over the data (general guidance, not legal advice). The more useful question is who controls the data and on what legal basis.

From conception to sustained use, with governance (p.10, p.12). Examples: ethics oversight in every phase of development (Solanki et al.), bias mitigation from data pre-processing to output post-processing, extra frameworks for trust, bias, explainability and ethics beyond existing acceptance models, and a governance model overseeing the whole process. The governance group should include software developers, government officials, health care staff, medical practitioners and patient advocates (Sunarti et al.), with clear accountability, for example who reviews an AI's X-ray reading. At national level, the paper calls for clear regulatory bodies, legal frameworks and clarity on liability for diagnostic errors.

Centre of the barriers. The authors say fairness, explainability and ethics 'seem to be' the centre of the barriers (p.11), an interpretation, not a measured result. Other papers this month point to practical barriers such as workflow fit, usability and staff time, so a fair answer is 'both': principled concerns shape trust, practical ones decide daily use.
Barriers and facilitators you have seen. No single answer; this one was for the group's own experience.

w2.summary: Sendak et al. describe how a deep learning sepsis alert, Sepsis Watch, was built and put into routine care at Duke, and show that most of the effort went into workflow design, relationships with clinicians and governance.
answers: Why rapid response nurses. Frontline emergency staff already had alarm fatigue from an earlier alert. Rapid response nurses could triage alerts across the hospital and call the right doctor (p.4).

Performance over interpretability. This is acceptable when the action is the same whatever the cause and a clinician confirms before acting, as with sepsis bundles. It is not acceptable when the AI's reason would change the treatment (p.6).

Who pays for 8000 hours in the NHS. The paper counts the time as an investment that built reusable infrastructure (p.11). In an NHS trust it would most likely sit with a digital or transformation budget. This NHS point is our suggestion, not from the paper.
Success or successful launch. A successful launch. The design is pre-post at a single site, and this paper reports no patient outcomes (p.10 to p.12).

Compared with Week 1. It confirms Hassan's points on workflow integration, trust built through clinical champions, and governance. It adds professional authority, that developers must not be seen as telling clinicians how to do their work (p.10).

An orthopaedic version. For example, an early warning for deterioration after hip fracture surgery, with alerts going to an orthogeriatric or outreach nurse, capped per hour, and overseen by a governance group from orthopaedics, geriatrics and nursing. This is a design idea, not a published tool.

w3.summary: Kawamoto et al. reviewed 70 randomised trials of clinical decision support and found four features linked to improved practice: support given automatically as part of the workflow, at the time and place of the decision, as a recommendation, and by computer.
answers: Odds ratio of 112 with no upper limit. Every trial without the feature failed to improve practice, so the association is strong but its size cannot be estimated. Quote it as a strong association, not as a precise number.
A binary outcome. It hides the effect size, so a tiny and a large improvement count the same.
71 comparisons and 18 variables. Treat the four features as a strong hypothesis. Over-fitting is possible, as the authors acknowledge.
Then and now. All four still map well onto AI tools. Automatic, in-workflow support is exactly how Sepsis Watch (Week 2) was designed.
Involvement. The two papers measure different things. Kawamoto looked at whether practice improved, while Sendak described what it took to get a tool adopted.
MSK. Most fracture detection tools meet three of the four features. The usual gap is the recommendation, because a box on the image is an assessment and does not say what to do next.
